requested.title: Push endpoint validation is not enforced when notifications are sent

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The stored endpoint is indeed only checked by `assertPublicHttpUrl` during registration, while `sendToSubscription` later passes it directly to `webpush.sendNotification`; no validated address is persisted or supplied to the send path. `web-push` 3.6.7 confirms that it performs a new DNS lookup through Node's `https.request`, so the registration-time DNS result is not a delivery-time pin. However, the route accepts only `https://` endpoints, and the dependency passes the original hostname to `https.request` without a custom agent, `rejectUnauthorized: false`, or custom certificate verifier. Node therefore performs normal certificate-chain and hostname validation before it can transmit the HTTP POST containing the push payload. A rebinding domain controlled by the attacker will resolve to the private IP at delivery, but an arbitrary internal service will not possess a certificate valid for that attacker-controlled hostname, so the TLS handshake fails and no HTTP request reaches the internal application. Repository-wide inspection found no project TLS override that disables this protection. The attacker could at most cause a TLS connection attempt/ClientHello to the rebinding target, not the claimed authenticated Web Push request to an arbitrary internal endpoint; a service already configured with a certificate for the attacker's domain would require separate control of that internal service. Git history shows the registration check was added in commit `c3e2b4e8`, and later commits did not add delivery pinning, but the stated critical SSRF exploit is blocked by HTTPS hostname verification.
